newsitem.title: USA: AOL reaches pact in class action lawsuit.
newsitem.headline: AOL reaches pact in class action lawsuit.

text.p: America Online Inc said on Thursday it has reached a preliminary agreement today in a nationally certified class action lawsuit that was filed against it due to its recent network connection problems.
AOL said that as part of its agreement, it will expand its refund and credit policy to cover subscribers who had difficulty connecting to the service in February and March.

The agreement provides refunds and credits upon written requests based on use for members who were online between two and 15 hours and experienced difficulty in connecting to AOL in either February or March.
The company did not specify any costs for the resolution of the nationwide class action, which was consolidated under one class in Circuit Court of Cook County, Illinois.

But a spokeswoman said that AOL believes the $24 million charge it took against second quarter earnings to pay for its refund settlement with the 36 state attorneys general in January will cover these refunds and credits for all members.
"We really see that the statement allows us to close the chapter on the access problem," an AOL spokeswoman said.
The class was represented by Ben Barnow and Larry Drury of Chicago and Lawrence Sucharow of New York.
The class action was certified in Illinois because plaintiff Steven Schwab, an AOL subscriber, filed the first class action suit against AOL in Cook County.

"This is a classwide settlement," said Ben Barnow, an attorney with Barnow & Goldberg, adding that the settlement must still be approved by the court and then it will be posted to the public via newspapers, the Internet and direct mailings. At that point, any AOL member can either remain as part of the class or they can opt out of the settlement.
"We feel this settlement brings substantial benefits to the class," Barnow said.

"This does really move us beyond the access issue," the AOL spokeswoman. "We are really making significant progress. We have put 75,000 modems in since January 1 and that has helped us have over 2.5 million more daily sessions."

AOL was besieged by complaints about network access problems after the company switched to offering customers unlimited access for a flat rate of $19.95 a month on December 1. Many members were so frustrated at not being able to sign on, or by difficulties in signing on, that they filed lawsuits against AOL.
